A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CoT-ICL Lab. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, experiments, equations, tables and figures can be matched despite renumbering and additions.

before.justification: v1 reports original transformer training experiments, controlled ablations, attention analyses and token-distribution analysis of CoT-Collection.

after.justification: v3 retains those results and adds pretrained-versus-random Llama experiments and a DeepSeek attention case study.

M1.justification: The DAG-based generator, MLP token processors, feature aggregation, training objectives and autoregressive evaluation remain substantively unchanged. Appendix A repairs mathematical expressions without establishing a different underlying algorithm; the additional models are experimental configurations.

E1.justification: The synthetic tasks and CoT-Collection analysis are retained. Section 7.2 adds one MMLU high-school mathematics question for a DeepSeek attention case study, a limited extension rather than evaluation across the MMLU benchmark.

E2.justification: Section 7.1 adds pretrained Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct versus a randomly initialized counterpart, each evaluated with and without CoT. Existing TF-4/8/12 comparisons remain; the additional related-work table entry is not an experimentally evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Existing synthetic training and evaluation settings are retained. New experiments introduce the 1B pretrained/random initialization comparison with vocabulary resized to 1024, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B generation with a 1024-token limit, temperatures 0.6 and 0.9, and attention thresholding at 0.001.

E4.justification: Section 7 adds focused analyses of whether NLP pretraining helps synthetic-task learning and whether a reasoning model exhibits sparse attention on a mathematics question. Appendix E supplies the prompt and responses. Existing synthetic ablations and attention analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The distribution-fitting analysis is retained, and neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed-based uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests for the model comparisons. The new temperature settings do not constitute uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Figure 10 adds a new comparison: pretrained/random Llama final accuracy is approximately 0.25/0.22 with CoT and 0.25/0.08 without CoT, with earlier transitions for the pretrained model. Figure 11 and Appendix E add sparse-attention observations and example responses. Original experimental curves are retained, including the reformatted v1 Figure 20a/v3 Figure 22a.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 corrects Equation (9)'s innermost layer from W_(L-1) to W_1. Algorithm 1 replaces E_data^T h_act with E_data h_act, repairing the dimensional mismatch for an embedding matrix of shape |V| by d. These are localized algebraic corrections; no new theoretical results or proofs appear.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about controllable synthetic CoT-ICL, accuracy transitions, model depth, context examples, embedding alignment and token-processor diversity. The added experiments support the existing NLP motivation without redefining the headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 7 newly interprets pretraining benefits as suggesting shared learned patterns between natural language and synthetic tasks, and sparse DeepSeek attention as motivation for sparse DAGs. The original limitation concerning ungrounded synthetic tokens and incomplete linguistic realism remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-repository link, describes vLLM/SGLang inference examples, and documents the new models' vocabulary resizing and generation settings. It also provides the exact mathematics prompt and responses and clarifies that 40 fixed processors comprise ten tuples of four MLPs. Existing hardware and training hyperparameters remain.

R1.justification: Expanded Appendix F explains relationships to real-valued ICL and Markov-chain-based tokenized settings. New references include Oko et al., Bietti et al., MMLU, vLLM and SGLang; Table 2 adds Oko et al. The main novelty positioning is retained.

P1.justification: The title replaces 'A Petri Dish' with 'A Synthetic Framework'; synthetic 'prompts' become 'sequences' throughout, with local prose corrections. Results receive a separate section, and the NLP connection and response appendix are added. Most existing exposition and its order remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with clearer grouping and labels. v3 adds Figures 10–11 and prompt/response Figures 30–32, expands Table 2, and reformats the axes and legends of the former Figure 20a. Most existing visual content is retained.

improvement.justification: The pretrained-versus-random comparison adds useful evidence for the framework's NLP motivation, while corrected formulas, clearer diagrams and code-access information improve usability and reproducibility. The gains remain limited: pretraining is evaluated on synthetic data, and the natural-language attention evidence covers one mathematics question without uncertainty estimates. The original limitation concerning synthetic-to-natural-language applicability is therefore only partly addressed.
